part_title: Neptune Knowledge Graphs, Redis Data Structures and GraphRAG

scenes.title: Amazon Neptune for knowledge graphs
scenes.narration: This slide models an insurance case as a network of connected facts. A customer is associated with a policy, a purchased product and an open incident. Instead of joining unrelated tables manually, the application can traverse relationships such as has-policy, covers and purchased-product to find the evidence needed for a question. The example asks whether a water-damage incident involving a sump pump is covered under the customer’s policy. Follow the traversal from customer to policy, from policy to covered categories, and from customer to product and incident. The generated answer cites the identified customer, policy, product and incident records. Neptune supports graph models and query languages suited to relationship-centric retrieval, including property-graph and RDF patterns. One caveat: the sample is simplified. Real insurance coverage depends on exclusions, timing, limits and policy wording, so a graph path alone does not prove a claim should be approved. Use graph traversal to retrieve verifiable related facts and apply business rules separately.

scenes.title: Redis data structures for AI apps
scenes.narration: This slide switches from relationships to low-latency structures that AI applications use during a conversation. A string key with TTL can hold a short-lived session summary or recent messages. A hash groups attributes such as user ID, current dialog stage and last-turn timestamp. A sorted set with timestamps or scores is useful for sliding-window rate limiting, where old entries are removed and recent events counted. The vector-oriented example illustrates a semantic cache: the application searches for a similar prior question before generating an answer, using the supported vector-search capability of the selected engine and version. Note the explicit time-to-live values and eviction policies. Session data, rate-limit records and response caches have different lifetimes and reliability needs; don't assign one default TTL to all of them. Not every Redis-compatible service or software version supports identical vector commands, so check your deployment. If state must be durable, distinguish MemoryDB or an appropriate persistent store from a disposable cache. Always partition keys and search results by tenant and security context.

scenes.title: Graph RAG with Neptune
scenes.narration: The GraphRAG flow begins with a natural-language question and identifies entities such as a disease, drug or side effect. The retrieval layer traverses relationships stored in Neptune and creates an evidence bundle consisting of specific entities, edges and supporting facts. The LLM receives this constrained context and produces an answer with traceable sources, rather than relying only on the model's internal memory. The diagram illustrates connections between Type 2 diabetes, medications and reported adverse effects. This is a conceptual example, not a medical recommendation: real-world claims require current clinical evidence, appropriate qualifiers and context. Focus on the architecture. Entity extraction must disambiguate names, the graph must remain current, traversal permissions must prevent exposing restricted information, and the prompt should avoid asserting facts beyond the retrieved paths. GraphRAG is strongest when the relationships themselves matter—for example ownership, dependencies, compliance rules or product compatibility. A conventional vector retriever may still be better for free-form text similarity, and both can be combined when needed.
